chunk_findings.detail: The handler throws away the output that the timed-out `communicate()` had already read, then re-reads only what is left after the kill. On POSIX, `subprocess.run` re-raises the *same* `TimeoutExpired` (its `output`/`stderr` hold "the output so far"; CPython comments this explicitly), so callers that surface `exc.stdout` to explain a gate/CI failure keep the command's output. `run_shell` does not: the inner loop's bare `raise` carries the partial bytes, but the outer handler ignores that exception, calls `_drain(p)`, and raises a brand-new `TimeoutExpired(..., output=out, stderr=err)`. Because the first `communicate()` already consumed the available bytes from the pipes, `_drain`'s second `p.communicate()` returns empty. Concretely, `subprocess.run("echo partial; sleep 30", shell=True, capture_output=True, timeout=1)` raises with `output=b'partial\n'`, while `proc.run_shell("echo partial; sleep 30", timeout=1)` raises with `output=b''` (and `stderr=b''`). Any caller that migrated from `P.run` and reports `e.stdout`/`e.stderr` will now print nothing. Fix: capture the inner exception (`except subprocess.TimeoutExpired as exc`) and re-raise it (optionally appending what `_drain` returns) instead of constructing a fresh one.

chunk_findings.detail: After a tick-driven `TimeoutExpired`, the remaining stdin is silently dropped and stdin is never closed, so a command that reads its input can never finish. The comment claims "already written: communicate keeps feeding the rest", but it does the opposite: it sets `data = None`, and on the next `p.communicate(input=None, ...)` CPython's `_communicate` only registers `self.stdin` for writing `if input:` and only closes stdin in the `not self._communication_started` branch, which is now False. The buffer that `input_view` had not yet written is gone, and EOF is never sent. Input that reproduces it: `run_shell("cat", input=b"x" * (1 << 20), timeout=None, on_tick=lambda: None, tick_s=1)` (or any command that consumes stdin slower than `tick_s`) — the first communicate times out mid-write, the retry writes nothing more and leaves the child's stdin open, so `cat` blocks forever and is only stopped when the deadline kills it, even though all of its input was supplied. Fix: keep the un-written remainder and/or close `p.stdin` in the retry path.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/proc.py run_shell (retry loop, `data = None`)

chunk_findings.detail:
The old call explicitly passed `stdin=subprocess.DEVNULL`:

```python
p = P.run(...,
    timeout=cfg.ci.timeout_s,
    stdin=subprocess.DEVNULL,
    check=False,
)
```

The new call drops it and passes no stdin equivalent. The other caller of the new shared helper — `gates.py` (`_run_ticking` and the non-ticking branch) — never set `stdin` before this change, so `run_shell` must inherit the parent's stdin to preserve *that* call site's behaviour; the helper therefore cannot be assumed to default to `DEVNULL` for the ci caller. Demonstrating input: with the operator's `[ci].command` set to something that reads stdin (e.g. `cat`, `read x`, or a tool that prompts), the process previously got immediate EOF and returned; now it inherits ddflow's stdin and blocks until `cfg.ci.timeout_s` expires, at which point the code returns `Result("unavailable", ...)` instead of the real (fast) result. This is an unrelated behavioural regression introduced by the refactor, and no test in the change covers stdin.

chunk_findings.detail: The module is guarded by `pytest.mark.skipif(os.name != "posix", ...)`, but the liveness check it relies on is Linux-only: `_alive` falls back to reading `/proc/{pid}/stat`, and on any non-Linux POSIX platform (macOS, the BSDs) that path does not exist, so `Path(...).read_text()` raises `OSError` and `_alive` returns `False` for a process that is in fact alive. Because `_alive` is the only thing `_gone` consults, `_gone` returns `True` on the first iteration on those platforms regardless of whether the grandchild was actually killed. Consequence: on macOS the three regression tests (`test_a_timed_out_command_gate_kills_its_grandchild`, `..._ticking_...`, `..._ci_...`) and `test_run_shell_raises_timeout_after_killing_the_group` all pass even against the unfixed `subprocess.run(..., shell=True, timeout=...)` code they are supposed to catch — the timeout fires, the orphaned `sleep 30` is still running, but `_gone` reports it gone. The test therefore provides no regression coverage outside Linux while still being selected there; it should either skip on non-Linux too (e.g. gate on `sys.platform == "linux"` / `Path("/proc").exists()`) or use a portable liveness probe (`os.waitpid`/`ps`) so the "gone" assertion can actually fail.

chunk_findings.detail:
On a tick-induced `subprocess.TimeoutExpired`, the handler unconditionally sets `data = None` and then loops back into `p.communicate(input=None, timeout=...)`. CPython's `Popen.communicate` refuses to accept input again once communication has started (`ValueError: Cannot send input after starting communication`), so this is why `data` is cleared — but clearing it means the *unwritten remainder* of the caller's `input` is silently dropped and is never delivered. Worse, because `_communication_started` is now True, the retry skips the `self.stdin.close()` branch and only registers stdin for writing when `input` is truthy, so `input=None` leaves stdin open and unregistered: the child blocks forever on its next read, is never sent EOF, and is only reaped when the hard deadline fires and `kill_group` SIGKILLs it. The inline comment `# already written: communicate keeps feeding the rest` is therefore false.

Concrete: `run_shell("cat", input=b"x" * (1 << 20), timeout=5, on_tick=lambda: None, tick_s=0.01)` writes roughly one pipe-buffer (≈64 KB) in the first `communicate`, the tick timeout fires, `data` becomes `None`, and `cat` never receives the remaining ~960 KB nor an EOF, so the call stalls until the 5 s deadline and then raises `TimeoutExpired` with truncated/absent output. The equivalent `subprocess.run("cat", shell=True, input=b"x" * (1 << 20), timeout=5)` returns returncode 0 with the full input echoed. The defect is latent for the gate/ci callers only because they do not currently pass `input`, but `run_shell` advertises `input` support and combines it with the `on_tick` path that triggers the loss.

chunk_findings.detail:
The old call passed `stdin=subprocess.DEVNULL`; the replacement call shown here passes only `command`, `timeout`, `cwd` and `text`, and nothing in the change adds `stdin=subprocess.DEVNULL`. The stated contract of the new `proc.run_shell` is only "start_new_session, killpg on timeout" — the other four pre-existing private copies it is modelled on (review.py, onboard_tests.py, onboard_verify.py, companions.py) are gate/command runners that never needed a null stdin, so run_shell has no reason to force one. If run_shell inherits `stdin` (the normal `subprocess.run` default, which is what gates.py relied on), the operator's `[ci].command` now runs with ddflow's stdin attached instead of `/dev/null`.

Concrete failure: operator sets `[ci].command = "read _; git merge-base ..."` (or any tool that reads stdin, e.g. a credential/confirmation prompt) and runs `ddflow` interactively. Before the change the child saw EOF on fd 0 and failed/returned immediately; now it blocks reading the terminal until `cfg.ci.timeout_s` elapses, at which point run_shell killpgs it and the command is reported as `"unavailable"` — a wrong status plus a multi-minute stall. If ddflow is instead driven with a pipe on stdin, the CI command silently consumes bytes that were meant for ddflow. This is exactly the kind of behavior that the existing tests (which use short, non-interactive commands) cannot catch.

chunk_findings.detail:
The liveness probe in `_alive` is Linux-specific: after `os.kill(pid, 0)` succeeds it reads `/proc/<pid>/stat` and interprets any `OSError` (including "no such file") as "process is dead":

```python
try:
    state = Path(f"/proc/{pid}/stat").read_text().rsplit(")", 1)[1].split()[0]
except OSError:
    return False
return state != "Z"
```

On any POSIX platform without procfs (macOS/BSD, which are not excluded by `pytestmark = pytest.mark.skipif(os.name != "posix", ...)` — only non-posix is skipped), `/proc/<pid>/stat` never exists, so `_alive` returns `False` for *every* pid, alive or dead. `_gone` therefore returns `True` on its first loop iteration without ever observing the grandchild, and all three timeout tests (`test_a_timed_out_command_gate_kills_its_grandchild`, `..._ticking_...`, `test_a_timed_out_ci_command_kills_its_grandchild`) plus `test_run_shell_raises_timeout_after_killing_the_group` pass on the *unfixed* code. Demonstrated input: `os.name == "posix"` and no `/proc` (e.g. macOS). Running `sleep 30 & echo $! > pf; wait` with the old `subprocess.run(shell=True, timeout=1)` leaves the `sleep` alive, but `_gone(pf)` still returns `True` because `_alive` short-circuits on the missing `/proc` file — so the regression test never fails on the code it is supposed to guard. The fix needs a probe that actually distinguishes a live pid (e.g. `ps -o stat=` or a waitpid/`kill(pid,0)` plus a zombie check that does not depend on procfs).

On POSIX, `subprocess.run` re-raises the *same* `TimeoutExpired` (its `output`/`stderr` hold "the output so far"; CPython comments this explicitly), so callers that surface `exc.stdout` to explain a gate/CI failure keep the command's output. `run_shell` does not: the inner loop's bare `raise` carries the partial bytes, but the outer handler ignores that exception, calls `_drain(p)`, and raises a brand-new `TimeoutExpired(..., output=out, stderr=err)`. Because the first `communicate()` already consumed the available bytes from the pipes, `_drain`'s second `p.communicate()` returns empty. Concretely, `subprocess.run("echo partial; sleep 30", shell=True, capture_output=True, timeout=1)` raises with `output=b'partial\n'`, while `proc.run_shell("echo partial; sleep 30", timeout=1)` raises with `output=b''` (and `stderr=b''`). Any caller that migrated from `P.run` and reports `e.stdout`/`e.stderr` will now print nothing. Fix: capture the inner exception (`except subprocess.TimeoutExpired as exc`) and re-raise it (optionally appending what `_drain` returns) instead of constructing a fresh one.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/proc.py run_shell (outer `except subprocess.TimeoutExpired`)

chunk_findings.detail: After a tick-driven `TimeoutExpired`, the remaining stdin is silently dropped and stdin is never closed, so a command that reads its input can never finish. The comment claims "already written: communicate keeps feeding the rest", but it does the opposite: it sets `data = None`, and on the next `p.communicate(input=None, ...)` CPython's `_communicate` only registers `self.stdin` for writing `if input:` and only closes stdin in the `not self._communication_started` branch, which is now False. The buffer that `input_view` had not yet written is gone, and EOF is never sent. Input that reproduces it: `run_shell("cat", input=b"x" * (1 << 20), timeout=None, on_tick=lambda: None, tick_s=1)` (or any command that consumes stdin slower than `tick_s`) — the first communicate times out mid-write, the retry writes nothing more and leaves the child's stdin open, so `cat` blocks forever and is only stopped when the deadline kills it, even though all of its input was supplied. Fix: keep the un-written remainder and/or close `p.stdin` in the retry path.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/proc.py run_shell (retry loop, `data = None`)

chunk_findings.detail:
The old call explicitly passed `stdin=subprocess.DEVNULL`:

```python
p = P.run(...,
    timeout=cfg.ci.timeout_s,
    stdin=subprocess.DEVNULL,
    check=False,
)
```

The new call drops it and passes no stdin equivalent. The other caller of the new shared helper — `gates.py` (`_run_ticking` and the non-ticking branch) — never set `stdin` before this change, so `run_shell` must inherit the parent's stdin to preserve *that* call site's behaviour; the helper therefore cannot be assumed to default to `DEVNULL` for the ci caller. Demonstrating input: with the operator's `[ci].command` set to something that reads stdin (e.g. `cat`, `read x`, or a tool that prompts), the process previously got immediate EOF and returned; now it inherits ddflow's stdin and blocks until `cfg.ci.timeout_s` expires, at which point the code returns `Result("unavailable", ...)` instead of the real (fast) result. This is an unrelated behavioural regression introduced by the refactor, and no test in the change covers stdin.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/ci.py:186 (the `P.run_shell(cmd, timeout=..., cwd=tree, text=True)` call)

chunk_findings.detail: The module is guarded by `pytest.mark.skipif(os.name != "posix", ...)`, but the liveness check it relies on is Linux-only: `_alive` falls back to reading `/proc/{pid}/stat`, and on any non-Linux POSIX platform (macOS, the BSDs) that path does not exist, so `Path(...).read_text()` raises `OSError` and `_alive` returns `False` for a process that is in fact alive. Because `_alive` is the only thing `_gone` consults, `_gone` returns `True` on the first iteration on those platforms regardless of whether the grandchild was actually killed. Consequence: on macOS the three regression tests (`test_a_timed_out_command_gate_kills_its_grandchild`, `..._ticking_...`, `..._ci_...`) and `test_run_shell_raises_timeout_after_killing_the_group` all pass even against the unfixed `subprocess.run(..., shell=True, timeout=...)` code they are supposed to catch — the timeout fires, the orphaned `sleep 30` is still running, but `_gone` reports it gone. The test therefore provides no regression coverage outside Linux while still being selected there; it should either skip on non-Linux too (e.g. gate on `sys.platform == "linux"` / `Path("/proc").exists()`) or use a portable liveness probe (`os.waitpid`/`ps`) so the "gone" assertion can actually fail.

chunk_findings.detail: The new docstring states "(stdin stays /dev/null)" and the new test asserts that `cat` must read EOF ("cat must read EOF from /dev/null, never our stdin"), but nothing in `run_shell` makes this true: the only stdin-related code was deleted (`kwargs.pop("input", None)` / `kwargs["stdin"] = PIPE`), and with `capture_output` only `stdout`/`stderr` are defaulted, so `popen(command, shell=True, **kwargs)` is called with `stdin=None`. `subprocess.Popen` with `stdin=None` does not redirect stdin — the child inherits the parent's fd 0. So when fd 0 is an open pipe or a tty (running the suite with `pytest -s`, executing the test module directly, or any caller of `run_shell` invoked from a terminal/agent whose stdin is not /dev/null), `P.run_shell("cat; echo done", cwd=tmp_path, timeout=10, text=True)` blocks in `cat` until the 10 s deadline and raises `subprocess.TimeoutExpired` instead of returning stdout `"done\n"`; if the inherited fd 0 is a pipe that later receives data, `cat` echoes it and the assertion fails with a different string. The test only passes today because the test harness happens to close/replace fd 0. The claim/behaviour mismatch is fixed by adding `kwargs.setdefault("stdin", subprocess.DEVNULL)` before the `popen(...)` call (or by deleting the claim and the test).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/proc.py `run_shell` (docstring claim and `test_run_shell_keeps_stdin_detached`)

chunk_findings.detail:
On a tick-induced `subprocess.TimeoutExpired`, the handler unconditionally sets `data = None` and then loops back into `p.communicate(input=None, timeout=...)`. CPython's `Popen.communicate` refuses to accept input again once communication has started (`ValueError: Cannot send input after starting communication`), so this is why `data` is cleared — but clearing it means the *unwritten remainder* of the caller's `input` is silently dropped and is never delivered. Worse, because `_communication_started` is now True, the retry skips the `self.stdin.close()` branch and only registers stdin for writing when `input` is truthy, so `input=None` leaves stdin open and unregistered: the child blocks forever on its next read, is never sent EOF, and is only reaped when the hard deadline fires and `kill_group` SIGKILLs it. The inline comment `# already written: communicate keeps feeding the rest` is therefore false.

Concrete: `run_shell("cat", input=b"x" * (1 << 20), timeout=5, on_tick=lambda: None, tick_s=0.01)` writes roughly one pipe-buffer (≈64 KB) in the first `communicate`, the tick timeout fires, `data` becomes `None`, and `cat` never receives the remaining ~960 KB nor an EOF, so the call stalls until the 5 s deadline and then raises `TimeoutExpired` with truncated/absent output. The equivalent `subprocess.run("cat", shell=True, input=b"x" * (1 << 20), timeout=5)` returns returncode 0 with the full input echoed. The defect is latent for the gate/ci callers only because they do not currently pass `input`, but `run_shell` advertises `input` support and combines it with the `on_tick` path that triggers the loss.

chunk_findings.detail:
The old call passed `stdin=subprocess.DEVNULL`; the replacement call shown here passes only `command`, `timeout`, `cwd` and `text`, and nothing in the change adds `stdin=subprocess.DEVNULL`. The stated contract of the new `proc.run_shell` is only "start_new_session, killpg on timeout" — the other four pre-existing private copies it is modelled on (review.py, onboard_tests.py, onboard_verify.py, companions.py) are gate/command runners that never needed a null stdin, so run_shell has no reason to force one. If run_shell inherits `stdin` (the normal `subprocess.run` default, which is what gates.py relied on), the operator's `[ci].command` now runs with ddflow's stdin attached instead of `/dev/null`.

Concrete failure: operator sets `[ci].command = "read _; git merge-base ..."` (or any tool that reads stdin, e.g. a credential/confirmation prompt) and runs `ddflow` interactively. Before the change the child saw EOF on fd 0 and failed/returned immediately; now it blocks reading the terminal until `cfg.ci.timeout_s` elapses, at which point run_shell killpgs it and the command is reported as `"unavailable"` — a wrong status plus a multi-minute stall. If ddflow is instead driven with a pipe on stdin, the CI command silently consumes bytes that were meant for ddflow. This is exactly the kind of behavior that the existing tests (which use short, non-interactive commands) cannot catch.

chunk_findings.detail:
The liveness probe in `_alive` is Linux-specific: after `os.kill(pid, 0)` succeeds it reads `/proc/<pid>/stat` and interprets any `OSError` (including "no such file") as "process is dead":

```python
try:
    state = Path(f"/proc/{pid}/stat").read_text().rsplit(")", 1)[1].split()[0]
except OSError:
    return False
return state != "Z"
```

On any POSIX platform without procfs (macOS/BSD, which are not excluded by `pytestmark = pytest.mark.skipif(os.name != "posix", ...)` — only non-posix is skipped), `/proc/<pid>/stat` never exists, so `_alive` returns `False` for *every* pid, alive or dead. `_gone` therefore returns `True` on its first loop iteration without ever observing the grandchild, and all three timeout tests (`test_a_timed_out_command_gate_kills_its_grandchild`, `..._ticking_...`, `test_a_timed_out_ci_command_kills_its_grandchild`) plus `test_run_shell_raises_timeout_after_killing_the_group` pass on the *unfixed* code. Demonstrated input: `os.name == "posix"` and no `/proc` (e.g. macOS). Running `sleep 30 & echo $! > pf; wait` with the old `subprocess.run(shell=True, timeout=1)` leaves the `sleep` alive, but `_gone(pf)` still returns `True` because `_alive` short-circuits on the missing `/proc` file — so the regression test never fails on the code it is supposed to guard. The fix needs a probe that actually distinguishes a live pid (e.g. `ps -o stat=` or a waitpid/`kill(pid,0)` plus a zombie check that does not depend on procfs).
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_gate_timeout_kills_group.py `_alive`

chunk_findings.detail: `run_shell` never sets `stdin` in `kwargs`, and `subprocess.Popen` defaults `stdin=None`, which means *inherit the parent's fd 0* — not `/dev/null`. The change removed the only `stdin` handling (`kwargs["stdin"] = PIPE` for `input=`) and added no replacement, so the new docstring ("stdin stays /dev/null") and the new regression test assert a detachment the code does not provide. The test only passes because pytest's default fd-capture installs `FDCapture(0)`, which points fd 0 at an empty temp file, so `cat; echo done` sees EOF. Run the same call where fd 0 is a terminal — e.g. `pytest -s tests/test_gate_timeout_kills_group.py::test_run_shell_keeps_stdin_detached`, or directly `P.run_shell("cat; echo done", timeout=10, text=True)` from an interactive shell — and `cat` blocks reading the tty until `timeout=10` fires, raising `TimeoutExpired` instead of returning `p.stdout == "done\n"`. Concretely: a gate/ci command that reads stdin (e.g. `python -c "input()"`, an interactive tool) inherits ddflow's stdin and can hang or consume operator input, contradicting the documented contract. The fix is to add `kwargs.setdefault("stdin", subprocess.DEVNULL)` (with the corresponding import) while still rejecting `input=`.

Review (by kilo)
------------------------------------------------------------
## Summary

Addresses the previous review's finding that `test_run_shell_keeps_stdin_detached` was a vacuous pass (pytest replaces fd 0 with `/dev/null`, so `cat` saw EOF whether or not `popen` set `stdin=DEVNULL`). The test now mirrors the established non-vacuous pattern in `tests/test_stdio_safety.py::test_the_guard_actually_detaches_stdin`: it spawns a parent process whose stdin is a real pipe carrying `PROTOCOL-BYTES\n`, has that parent call `P.run_shell('cat; echo done', ...)`, then read its own stdin. With the guard, the child gets `DEVNULL` and the parent retains its bytes; without it, `cat` swallows the protocol bytes and both assertions fail. The diff correctly achieves the commit message's intent.

Verification of the finding: I traced the data flow — `run_shell` passes no `stdin`, so the default at `ddflow/infra/proc.py:58` is the only thing detaching fd 0; removing it makes `cat` inherit the pipe and consume the bytes, failing `CHILD_SAW='done\n'` and `PARENT_KEPT='PROTOCOL-BYTES\n'`. The test is therefore mutation-proof, and it exercises `run_shell`/`popen` (the path the prior review noted was untested), not just `P.run`. The assertion strings are correct (`repr` of `'done\n'` yields the literal `\n` matched by `"CHILD_SAW='done\\n'"`).
